title: Who is closest?
summary: Relatedness comes from shared ancestry — the node where two lineages last met — not from how close tips sit on the page or how alike the organisms look.

objectives: Find a tip's closest relative as the lineage sharing its most recent common ancestor
Read a polytomy as 'the tree does not say which split came first'
Tell relatedness apart from resemblance and from tip order on the page

items.note_after: A tip's closest relative is its sister: whatever shares its most recent node.

items.text: Tap one of {a}'s closest relatives — the sister may be a whole clade, not a single tip.
items.note_after: {a}'s sister is the whole rodent clade: every tip in it shares the same most recent common ancestor with {a}.

items.text: Is {a} more closely related to {b} or to {c}, or is it equally close to both?
items.note_after: Shared ancestry decides: {a} and {b} meet at a node that {c} does not descend from.

items.text: Is {a} more closely related to {b} or to {c}, or is it equally close to both?
items.note_after: All three lineages meet at the same polytomy — the tree does not say which two split first, so {a} is equally close to both.

items.text: Tap every tip most distant from {a}.
items.note_after: The most distant tips sit beyond {a}'s side of the deepest split — here, the whole other clade.
{a} is shaped like a fish, but shared ancestry decides relatedness: its lineage meets the birds' lineage before it meets any fish.

items.text: Is {a} more closely related to {b} or to {c} — and why?

reasons: Their lineages meet at a more recent common ancestor than either shares with the other taxon.
They look more alike — the streamlined swimmers must be closest.
